after.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
after.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 2}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{1}=2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-1)}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-3)^{2}+(3-3)^{2}+(-5-(-3))^{2}+(2-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The projection coefficients are (x·a₁)/(a₁·a₁)=14/14=1 and (x·a₂)/(a₂·a₂)=13/13=1. Thus proj_S(x)=a₁+a₂=(5,1,0,−1), with squared norm 27. Since ‖x‖²=63, the acute angle is arccos(√(27/63))≈49.11°.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
after.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{5\cdot 3+5\cdot 0+2\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{5\cdot 2+5\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+3\cdot (-2)}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}\,x}{‖x‖\,‖{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x‖} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 5+5\cdot 1+2\cdot 0+3\cdot (-1)}{\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{27}{\sqrt{63}\sqrt{27}} \\  & =\frac{27}{3\sqrt{7}\cdot 3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{21}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{21}}{7})≈{49.11}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

after.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
after.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{3\cdot 1+4\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot 1+2\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{3\cdot 2+4\cdot (-1)+(-3)\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{3\cdot 7+4\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 5}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{7}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{5}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{38}{\sqrt{38}\sqrt{76}} \\  & =\frac{38}{38\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
after.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{0\cdot 1+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}v=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
content.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
content.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{0\cdot 1+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}v=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
